title: Logistic Regression Hurt by Symmetric Label Noise Still Flags Most Flipped Labels Out of Fold
insight: Logistic regression weakened by symmetric label noise still disagrees, out of fold, with most of the flipped labels, and dropping those disagreements before one refit wins back much of the lost accuracy on average in three of our four noisy settings.
abstract_sketch: Symmetric label noise costs logistic regression accuracy, yet predictions from the same kind of classifier, made on samples held out from its fit, disagree with most of the flipped labels. We turn this into a one-pass filter that drops every training sample whose out-of-fold prediction disagrees with its given label and refits on the rest, with no clean validation set, noise-rate estimate, or confidence threshold. On two small datasets with noisy training labels, most dropped samples are mislabeled, a far higher share than in the training set as a whole. On seed means, the refit model wins back much of the lost accuracy on digits at both noise rates and on breast cancer at the lower rate, but only a small part on breast cancer at the higher rate. The price is that correct samples are discarded too (the filter removes up to about half of the training set at the higher rate), while with clean labels its mean accuracy is only a fraction of a point below that of plain logistic regression.
figure1: One full-width figure at the top of page 1, in three panels, readable without the text. (a) 'One pass': a schematic stack of training samples with given labels, a few of them flipped, passing through four numbered stages with short plain labels: 1 'Predict out of fold', 2 'Compare labels', 3 'Drop mismatches', 4 'Refit'. The dropped pile holds mostly flipped samples and also a correct one, and one flipped sample slips through. The caption says the samples are schematic because no per-sample outputs were saved. (b) 'What gets dropped': for each of the four noisy settings (two datasets, two noise rates), grouped bars give the share of flipped labels that are dropped and the share of dropped samples that are flipped, with a gray bar for the share of flipped labels in the whole training set; bars are means over 5 seeds with sd error bars and seed points. The reader sees that both shares are high and that the drops are far richer in flipped labels than the training set. (c) 'What comes back': test accuracy in the same four settings for clean-label logistic regression (gray reference), logistic regression on all noisy labels (partner color), and ours (accent), with paired seed points joined by thin lines. The reader sees noise open a gap, filtering close much of it on average in three settings but not all of it, and only a small part come back on breast cancer at the higher rate, where seeds also spread widely. The caption's first sentence states the idea and the rest walks through the three panels, including the weak case.
contributions: We show on two small datasets that out-of-fold predictions of logistic regression under symmetric label noise disagree with most flipped labels, and that most of these disagreements are truly mislabeled, although correctly labeled samples are flagged too.

We describe a one-pass filter that drops the disagreements and refits the linear model, with fixed folds and regularization and with no clean validation set, noise-rate estimate, or confidence threshold.

We measure what the refit model gains and costs: accuracy under noisy labels, including the setting where little is recovered and the gap that remains to clean-label training, and the small mean cost on clean labels.
storyline: On two small datasets, symmetric label noise lowers the accuracy of logistic regression, and the higher rate lowers it further. The same kind of classifier still gives a useful check on its own training labels: when each sample is predicted by a model fit without it, the disagreements include most of the flipped labels and are far richer in them than the training set as a whole. The method follows directly, since we drop the disagreements and refit once, and by design it needs no clean validation set and no noise-rate estimate. On seed means the refit model wins back much of the lost accuracy in three of the four noisy settings and only a small part on breast cancer at the higher rate, and it remains below clean-label training at the higher rate on both datasets and at the lower rate on breast cancer. The price is measured as well: correct samples are discarded, a large part of the training set goes at the higher rate, and on clean labels every drop is a correct sample even though mean accuracy barely falls. In the settings we test, one cross-validation pass is enough to find most flipped labels, which leaves keeping the correct samples and closing the remaining gap as the open problems.

sections.title: Method: One Pass of Out-of-Fold Filtering
Out-of-fold disagreements catch most flipped labels and are mostly mislabeled
Correct samples are dropped too, and heavier noise changes what is caught
Refitting wins back much of the lost accuracy, with a clear weak case
With clean labels, mean accuracy barely falls although every drop is a correct sample
The lead over a small MLP does not isolate the effect of filtering

risks: First, a reviewer will say that out-of-fold filtering is close to classification filtering and confident learning. The paper claims no new method or priority, presents both as close relatives that were not run here, and offers a measured account of what one pass drops and what accuracy it returns. Second, high recall could come from dropping a large part of the data. The paper reports drop precision beside the flipped share of the whole training set, which shows that the drops are enriched in flipped labels. It does not claim that the accuracy gain comes from this choice, because no random-drop or oracle control was run. Third, finding wrong labels with a model trained on partly correct ones may look expected under symmetric noise. The paper offers the size of the effect and its limits as measurements: fewer flips are caught at the higher rate, correct samples are lost, and a gap to clean-label training remains. Fourth, recovery is partial and uneven. The abstract, Figure 1 and the results state the weak case on breast cancer at the higher rate and quote recovery as a ratio of seed means. A share above one half is claimed as tested only on digits at the lower rate; on digits at the higher rate and breast cancer at the lower rate it holds on seed means but the tests do not establish it. The lower-rate gain on breast cancer is reported as a higher mean that five seeds do not establish. Fifth, the study is small, with two datasets, synthetic noise, and seeds that re-split the same data. The scope is stated up front, paired seed values are shown, tests are treated as descriptive, and nothing is said about deep networks or large data. Sixth, the MLP comparison could be read as support for filtering. The paper states that plain logistic regression also beats this untuned MLP under noise, so the gap is not counted as a contribution.
